On module endomorphisms annihilated by residually square-free polynomials over Artinian local PIRs

Abdelghaffar Chibloun ††thanks: E-mail: ab.chibloun@edu.umi.ac.ma Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, FS–Meknes, Moulay Ismail University, Meknes, Morocco    Mustapha Najmeddine ††thanks: E-mail: m.najmeddine@umi.ac.ma Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, ENSAM–Meknes, Moulay Ismail University, Meknes, Morocco
Abstract

We consider finitely generated free modules and their endomorphisms over an Artinian local PIR, also known as an SPIR. We characterize submodules of such modules by constructing minimal generating sets from given bases. We prove that any endomorphism possessing a square-free annihilating polynomial modulo the maximal ideal admits a principal annihilating ideal, and establish that every free invariant submodule under such an endomorphism has an invariant complement. Moreover, for such endomorphisms, we detail the construction of invariant submodules and compute the number of free invariant submodules when the ring is finite. Furthermore, we introduce canonical matrices associated with these endomorphisms, yielding a complete characterization of matrix similarity via invariant polynomials in this context. Finally, we address the non-derogatory case, obtaining a sharper characterization of submodule invariance.

Keywords– Artinian local PIR, Special principal ideal ring (SPIR), Module endomorphisms, Square-free polynomials, Invariant submodules, Matrix similarity

Mathematics Subject Classification (2020) – 13E10, 13F10, 13C05, 15B33, 15A21

1 Introduction

A special principal ideal ring (SPIR) is a commutative principal ideal ring (PIR) having exactly one prime ideal. It is obviously local and Noetherian. Moreover, as it has Krull dimension 0, it is an Artinian local PIR. Conversely, every Artinian local PIR is an SPIR. Indeed, as such a ring has Krull dimension 0, each of its prime ideals is maximal, hence as it is local, it has only one prime ideal. SPIRs play a significant role in commutative algebra, mainly due to the Zariski–Samuel Structure Theorem for PIRs [25, Volume 1, Chapter 4, Theorem 33], which states that every PIR is isomorphic to a finite direct product of PIDs and SPIRs. They arise naturally in several classical contexts. Prominent examples include finite chain rings—such as Galois rings GR​(pn,r)\text{GR}(p^{n},r) (which reduce to ℤ/pn​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p^{n}\mathbb{Z} when r=1r=1) and their Eisenstein extensions (see [13, Theorem XVII.5 ])—as well as quotients of the form k⁡[x]/(fn)k[x]/(f^{n}), where kk is a field and f∈k⁡[x]f\in k[x] is irreducible.

Study of matrices with coefficients in an SPIR has attracted considerable attention over several decades. Davis [6] showed that over ℤ/pn​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p^{n}\mathbb{Z}, the similarity of two square matrices reduces to the similarity of their reductions modulo p,p, provided both matrices satisfy a common polynomial whose reduction modulo pp is square-free. McDonald [14] developed the general theory of similarity over SPIRs and demonstrated that a ”rational” canonical form is available for a suitable class of matrices, however, a counterexample was later given by Guralnick in [8]. Nechaev [17] subsequently classified the similarity classes of square matrices of order 33 over ℤ/p2​ℤ.\mathbb{Z}/p^{2}\mathbb{Z}. Kurakin [11] established a structured approach to classify similarity over SPIRs by associating to each matrix a system of polynomial ideals over a discrete valuation ring that remains invariant under similarity transformations. Avni [1] analyzed the similarity classes of 3×33\times 3 matrices over a local PIR, producing a classification of representatives and an explicit enumeration in the case where the residue field is finite. Prasad [21] developed a theory of normal forms for similarity classes over an SPIR of length two, and described the similarity classes for square matrices with order at most 4.4. However, despite this progress, the classification of similarity classes over SPIRs remains incomplete in general: existing results either restrict the length of the ring, the size of the matrices, or the class of endomorphisms considered.

On the other hand, the study of invariant submodules of an endomorphism is central to module theory and linear algebra, providing a structural framework to break down complex algebraic systems into simpler components. Formally, given a module MM and an endomorphism φ\varphi, a submodule N≤MN\leq M is φ\varphi-invariant if it satisfies φ⁡(N)⊆N.\varphi(N)\subseteq N. When a module can be decomposed into a direct sum of invariant submodules, the endomorphism can be represented in a block diagonal matrix form, which is easier to work with. The study of invariant submodules has also proved to be useful in coding theory where, for example, polycyclic codes can be seen as invariant submodules of a certain endomorphism of RnR^{n} (see [22, 23, 2, 20]).

In this paper, we investigate a class of endomorphisms of finitely generated free modules over an SPIR, namely, those with annihilating polynomials that are square-free modulo the maximal ideal.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews basic definitions and properties of module endomorphisms over commutative rings, alongside foundational results on local and principal ideal rings used throughout. Section 3 establishes useful results concerning polynomials and finitely generated free modules over Artinian rings. In Section 4, we describe properties of SPIRs and characterize submodules of finitely generated free modules by constructing minimal generating sets from a given basis. In Section 5, we demonstrate that over an SPIR, an endomorphism of a finitely generated free module possesses a principal annihilating ideal, provided its annihilating polynomial is square-free modulo the maximal ideal. We also prove that every free invariant submodule under such an endomorphism admits an invariant complement. Continuing the study of such endomorphisms, Section 6 investigates their invariant submodules, detailing their construction from a given module basis and calculating the total number of free invariant submodules in the finite ring case. Additionally, we introduce associated canonical matrices for these endomorphisms, allowing us to characterize matrix similarity via polynomial invariants in this context. Finally, Section 7 addresses the non-derogatory case where a sharper characterization of invariance is given.

We conclude this preliminary section with a collection of essential results on modules over local and principal ideal rings that will be used throughout the remainder of the paper.

Theorem 1.

([12, Theorem 2.3]) Let (R,𝔪,k)(R,\mathfrak{m},k) be a local ring and MM a finitely generated RR-module. M/𝔪​MM/\mathfrak{m}M is a finite-dimensional vector space over kk, and we write nn for its dimension.

  • (i)

    If we take a basis {u1+𝔪​M,…,un+𝔪​M}\{u_{1}+\mathfrak{m}M,\dots,u_{n}+\mathfrak{m}M\} of M/𝔪​MM/\mathfrak{m}M over kk, then {u1,…,un}\{u_{1},\dots,u_{n}\} is a minimal generating set of MM;

  • (ii)

    conversely every minimal generating set of MM is obtained in this way, and so has nn elements.

  • (iii)

    If {u1,…,un}\{u_{1},\dots,u_{n}\} and {v1,…,vn}\{v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\} are both minimal generating sets of M,M, and vi=∑ai​j​uiv_{i}=\sum a_{ij}u_{i} with ai​j∈Ra_{ij}\in R then det​(ai​j)\text{det}(a_{ij}) is a unit of R,R, so that (ai​j)(a_{ij}) is an invertible matrix.

We have then, that over a local ring R,R, for a finitely generated RR-module M,M, every minimal generating set of MM has the same cardinality. We call the minimal number of generators of MM and denote it νR​(M).\nu_{R}(M). An immediate consequence of Theorem 1, is that for any two finitely generated RR-modules MM and N,N, νR​(M⊕N)=νR​(M)+νR​(N).\nu_{R}(M\oplus N)=\nu_{R}(M)+\nu_{R}(N).

Proposition 1.

([12, Theorem 2.5.]) Let (R,𝔪)(R,\mathfrak{m}) be a local ring, then a projective module over RR is free.

Lemma 1.

[14, Lemma II.2] Let (R,𝔪)(R,\mathfrak{m}) be a local ring and FF a finitely generated free RR-module. If {x1,…,xn}\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\} is a minimal generating set of F,F, then it is linearly independent.

Using Theorem 1, Lemma 1 and the incomplete basis theorem for vector spaces, an immediate corollary is that we can ”transfer” linear independence from the residue field over to the ring. Namely we have the following:

Corollary 1.

Let (R,𝔪,k)(R,\mathfrak{m},k) be a local ring and FF a finitely generated free RR-module. Let u1,…​uru_{1},\dots u_{r} be elements in F.F. If {u1+𝔪​F,…,ur+𝔪​F}\{u_{1}+\mathfrak{m}F,\dots,u_{r}+\mathfrak{m}F\} is linearly independent in F/𝔪​FF/\mathfrak{m}F then {u1,…,ur}\{u_{1},\dots,u_{r}\} is linearly independent and can be completed into a basis of F.F.

3 Some useful results on Artinian local rings

Let RR be an Artinian local ring with maximal ideal 𝔪.\mathfrak{m}. In this section, we present some results concerning polynomials over RR as well as finitely generated RR-modules that will be useful throughout the paper.

Let ff and gg be two polynomials in R⁡[x].R[x]. ff is said to be regular if it is not a zero divisor, which is the case if and only if it has a non-zero-divisor coefficient. It is said to be basic irreducible if μ⁡(f)\mu(f) is an irreducible polynomial in k⁡[x].k[x]. ff is said to be square-free if it is not divisible by the square of any non-constant polynomial in R⁡[x],R[x], moreover, it is called residually square-free if μ⁡(f)\mu(f) is square-free in k⁡[x].k[x]. Finally, ff and gg are said to be coprime if (f,g)=R⁡[x].(f,g)=R[x]. As RR is Artinian, by Nakayama’s Lemma 𝔪\mathfrak{m} is nilpotent, and is in fact the nilradical of R.R. A ring whose nilradical is a maximal ideal is called a completely primary ring. Through a series of papers in the 50s, Snapper described the polynomial ideals over this type of rings. Namely the following result follows a characterization that appears on [24, Section 12].

Lemma 2.

([24, Section 12])

  • (a)

    Let ff be a regular polynomial in R⁡[x].R[x]. Then there exists a monic polynomial g∈R⁡[x]g\in R[x] and a unit polynomial u∈R⁡[x]u\in R[x] such that f=u​g.f=ug.

  • (b)

    Let I⊴R⁡[x]I\unlhd R[x] be an ideal such that μ⁡(I)≠(0).\mu(I)\neq(0). There exists a monic polynomial f∈If\in I with least degree among the monic polynomials of II such that I=(f,N)I=(f,N) where N=I∩𝔪⁡[x].N=I\cap\mathfrak{m}[x].

Using the previous result, it is easy to see that over an Artinian local ring, we have Euclidean division provided that the divisor is regular.

Lemma 3.

(Euclidean division) Let ff and gg be two nonzero polynomials in R⁡[x].R[x]. If gg is regular then there exist polynomials qq and rr in R⁡[x]R[x] with f=q​g+rf=qg+r and deg⁡(r)<deg⁡(g).\deg(r)<\deg(g).

Proposition 2.

Let I⊴R⁡[x]I\unlhd R[x] be an ideal such that μ⁡(I)≠(0),\mu(I)\neq(0), and let f,g∈If,g\in I be two monic polynomials of least degree among the monic polynomials in I.I. We have then f−g∈I∩𝔪⁡[x].f-g\in I\cap\mathfrak{m}[x]. In particular μ⁡(f)=μ⁡(g).\mu(f)=\mu(g).

Proof.

Following Lemma 2, let I=(f0,N)I=(f_{0},N) with f0f_{0} monic, deg⁡(f0)=deg⁡(f)\deg(f_{0})=\deg(f) and N=I∩𝔪⁡[x].N=I\cap\mathfrak{m}[x]. By Euclidean division, we have f=q​g+rf=qg+r with q,r∈R⁡[x]q,r\in R[x] and deg⁡(r)<deg⁡(g).\deg(r)<\deg(g). But as ff and gg are monic with the same degree, they have the same leading term, hence q=1q=1 and f−g=r∈I.f-g=r\in I. Let α∈R⁡[x]\alpha\in R[x] and β∈N\beta\in N such that r=α​f0+β.r=\alpha f_{0}+\beta. If α∉𝔪⁡[x],\alpha\notin\mathfrak{m}[x], then the sum r=α​f0+βr=\alpha f_{0}+\beta has a term of degree at least deg⁡(f0),\deg(f_{0}), but as deg⁡(r)<deg⁡(g)=deg⁡(f0)\deg(r)<\deg(g)=\deg(f_{0}) we must have α∈𝔪⁡[x],\alpha\in\mathfrak{m}[x], and thus f−g=r∈N=I∩𝔪⁡[x].f-g=r\in N=I\cap\mathfrak{m}[x]. ∎

It is a well-known fact that an Artinian local ring is complete. We have therefore, by [12, Theorem 8.3], RR is a Henselian ring, i.e. a local ring in which Hensel’s lemma holds.

Proposition 3.

(Hensel’s lemma) Let f⁡(x)∈R⁡[x]f(x)\in R[x] be a monic polynomial and let μ⁡(f)=∏i=1rgi,\mu(f)=\prod^{r}_{i=1}g_{i}, where g1,…,gr∈k⁡[x]g_{1},\dots,g_{r}\in k[x] are monic, pairwise coprime. Then there exist monic, pairwise coprime polynomials f1,…,fr∈R⁡[x]f_{1},\dots,f_{r}\in R[x] such that f=∏i=1rfif=\prod^{r}_{i=1}f_{i} and μ⁡(fi)=gi\mu(f_{i})=g_{i} for 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r.

Although we do not have unique factorization in R⁡[x]R[x] in general, the next proposition shows that residually square-free polynomials behave favorably in this regard.

Proposition 4.

A residually square-free monic polynomial in R⁡[x]R[x] factors uniquely into monic, pairwise coprime basic irreducible polynomials.

Proof.

The existence of such a decomposition follows directly from Hensel’s lemma. The proof of the uniqueness is similar to that given in [13, Theorem XIII.11] for finite local rings. ∎

The next lemma is given in [19, Lemma 2.8] for the case of finite chain rings. The proof is the same for Artinian local rings.

Lemma 4.

Let ff and gg be two regular polynomials in R⁡[x]R[x]. Then ff and gg are coprime if and only if μ⁡(f)\mu(f) and μ⁡(g)\mu(g) are coprime polynomials in k⁡[x]k[x].

While no additional condition is required on a local ring for the generating property of a subset to be transferred via μ\mu and vice-versa as seen in Theorem 1, the transfer of linear independence needs more. It turns out, as we will see in Proposition 5, that for a local ring to have this linear independence transfer property, it needs to satisfy a sort of incomplete basis property. A ring SS is said to be weakly semi-Steinitz, if every linearly independent finite subset of a finitely generated free SS-module FF can be extended to a basis of F.F. See [15, 5] for more details about weakly semi-Steinitz and Steinitz rings in general. In particular, [15, Corollary 2.5.] states that a commutative Noetherian ring is weakly semi-Steinitz if and only if every non-zero-divisor is a unit, hence it is clear that an Artinian local ring is weakly semi-Steinitz. As a consequence, we have the following straightforward properties.

Proposition 5.

Let FF be a finitely generated free RR-module. We have the following:

  • (i)

    If {w1,…,wr}\{w_{1},\dots,w_{r}\} is a linearly independent subset of F,F, then {w1+𝔪​F,…,wr+𝔪​F}\{w_{1}+\mathfrak{m}F,\dots,w_{r}+\mathfrak{m}F\} is linearly independent in F/𝔪​F.F/\mathfrak{m}F.

  • (ii)

    Each linearly independent subset of FF with cardinality rankR⁡(F)\operatorname{rank}_{R}(F) is a basis of F.F.

  • (iii)

    For any free submodule VV of F,F, VV is a direct summand of F.F.

Remark 1.

Let FF be a finitely generated free RR-module and MM a free submodule of F.F. μ⁡(M)\mu(M) may refer to two objects: the image of MM under the projection μ:F⟶F/𝔪​F,\mu:F\longrightarrow F/\mathfrak{m}F, or M/𝔪​MM/\mathfrak{m}M the image of the induced projection μ:M⟶M/𝔪​M\mu:M\longrightarrow M/\mathfrak{m}M as in diagram 1. However, as RR is weakly semi-Steinitz, from Proposition 5(iii) MM is a direct summand of F,F, hence the natural map M/𝔪​M→F/𝔪​FM/\mathfrak{m}M\rightarrow F/\mathfrak{m}F is injective and the two objects coincide.

Proposition 6.

Let FF be a finitely generated free RR-module and φ∈EndR​(F).\varphi\in\text{End}_{R}(F). Let W≤FW\leq F be a free submodule invariant under φ.\varphi. Then χφ↾W{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi_{\restriction W}} divides χφ.{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi}. As RR is weakly semi-Steinitz, from Proposition 5(iii), WW is a direct summand of F.F. Let F=W⊕W′F=W\oplus W^{\prime} where W′W^{\prime} is some free submodule of F.F. Let ℬ\mathcal{B} and ℬ′\mathcal{B^{\prime}} be bases of WW and W′W^{\prime} respectively. As WW is φ\varphi-invariant, φ\varphi is represented in the ordered basis ℬ∪ℬ′\mathcal{B}\cup\mathcal{B^{\prime}} as a matrix A=(BC0D),A=\begin{pmatrix}B&C\\ 0&D\end{pmatrix}, with BB the matrix of φ↾W\varphi_{\restriction W} in ℬ.\mathcal{B}. It follows that d​e​t​(x​I−A)=d​e​t​(x​I−B)​d​e​t​(x​I−D),det(xI-A)=det(xI-B)det(xI-D), and thus χφ↾W{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi_{\restriction W}} divides χφ{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi} (note that II denotes different identity matrices in the previous by abuse of notation). Moreover, if W′W^{\prime} is also φ\varphi-invariant, then C=0C=0 and DD is the matrix of φ↾W′\varphi_{\restriction W^{\prime}} in ℬ′.\mathcal{B^{\prime}}. Hence d​e​t​(x​I−D)=χφ↾W′det(xI-D)={\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi_{\restriction W^{\prime}}} and χφ=χφ↾W​χφ↾W′.{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi}={\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi_{\restriction W}}{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi_{\restriction W^{\prime}}}. ∎

4 Finitely generated free modules over an SPIR

In this section, we describe the structure of submodules of a finitely generated free module over an Artinian local principal ideal ring. We start with some useful results concerning the structure of these rings. For a detailed discussion about SPIRs see [25, Volume 1, Chapter 4, Section 15]. Let RR be an SPIR with maximal ideal 𝔪,\mathfrak{m}, and let γ∈R\gamma\in R such that 𝔪=(γ).\mathfrak{m}=(\gamma). As RR is Artinian, the ideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m} is nilpotent. Let ν∈ℕ∗\nu\in\mathbb{N}^{*} denote the nilpotency index of 𝔪.\mathfrak{m}. The ideals of RR form a strictly increasing chain

(0)=𝔪ν⊊𝔪ν−1⊊⋯⊊𝔪⊊R.(0)=\mathfrak{m}^{\nu}\subsetneq\mathfrak{m}^{\nu-1}\subsetneq\dots\subsetneq\mathfrak{m}\subsetneq R\,. (2)
Lemma 5.

Let FF be a finitely generated free RR-module. For any element w∈F∖{0},w\in F\setminus\{0\}, there is a unique integer ss and an element w′∈F∖𝔪​Fw^{\prime}\in F\setminus\mathfrak{m}F such that w=γs​w′,w=\gamma^{s}w^{\prime}, where 0≤s≤ν−1.0\leq s\leq\nu-1.

Proof.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that F≃RRn,F\simeq_{R}R^{n}, and let (w1,…,wn)∈Rn∖{0}(w_{1},\dots,w_{n})\in R^{n}\setminus\{0\} be the vector corresponding to ww in Rn.R^{n}. For each 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n such that wi≠0,w_{i}\neq 0, by [18, Proposition 2.2], there exists a unique sis_{i} and a unit ui∈Ru_{i}\in R such that wi=ui​γsi.w_{i}=u_{i}\gamma^{s_{i}}. The result follows then by taking ss to be min1≤i≤n⁡{si}.\min_{1\leq i\leq n}\{s_{i}\}. ∎

Lemma 6.

Let FF be a finitely generated free RR-module. Then for each w∈F,w\in F, if 1≤i≤j≤ν1\leq i\leq j\leq\nu and γi​w∈𝔪j​F\gamma^{i}w\in\mathfrak{m}^{j}F then w∈𝔪j−i​F.w\in\mathfrak{m}^{j-i}F.

Proof.

Follows as in the case of finite chain rings presented in [19, Section 2.3]. ∎

The next result was given in [7, 3.1 Lemma] for the case of finite chain rings. We present it here for SPIRs with a shorter proof.

Proposition 7.

Let f∈R⁡[x]f\in R[x] be a basic irreducible polynomial. Then R⁡[x]/(f)R[x]/(f) is an SPIR, with nilpotency index ν,\nu, and ideals

(0)⊊(γν−1+(f))⊊⋯⊊(γ+(f))⊊R⁡[x]/(f).(0)\subsetneq(\gamma^{\nu-1}+(f))\subsetneq\dots\subsetneq(\gamma+(f))\subsetneq R[x]/(f)\,. (3)
Proof.

By Lemma 2, we may assume ff is monic w.l.o.g. Let I⊴R⁡[x]I\unlhd R[x] be an ideal containing f,f, and let f1,…,fqf_{1},\dots,f_{q} be such that I=(f1,…,fq).I=(f_{1},\dots,f_{q}). For all i,i, let ri∈R⁡[x]r_{i}\in R[x] be the rest of the Euclidean division of fif_{i} by f.f. If ri=0r_{i}=0 let λi=ν.\lambda_{i}=\nu. Otherwise, let λi∈ℕ\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{N} and ri∗∈R⁡[x]r^{*}_{i}\in R[x] regular such that ri=γλi​ri∗r_{i}=\gamma^{\lambda_{i}}r^{*}_{i} and deg​(ri)=deg​(ri∗).\text{deg}(r_{i})=\text{deg}(r^{*}_{i}). As μ⁡(f)\mu(f) is basic irreducible and deg⁡(μ⁡(ri∗))<deg⁡(f),\deg(\mu(r^{*}_{i}))<\deg(f), μ⁡(ri∗)\mu(r^{*}_{i}) and μ⁡(f)\mu(f) are coprime, hence by Lemma 4, ri∗r^{*}_{i} and ff are coprime, which means that ri∗r^{*}_{i} is a unit modulo f.f. Hence, I/(f)=(γλ1+(f),…,γλq+(f))=(γm​i​n​{λi}i+(f)).I/(f)=(\gamma^{\lambda_{1}}+(f),\dots,\gamma^{\lambda_{q}}+(f))=(\gamma^{min\{\lambda_{i}\}_{i}}+(f)). Furthermore, as RR can naturally be embedded in R⁡[x]/(f),R[x]/(f), the nilpotency index cannot be less than ν,\nu, which implies that it equals ν\nu and that the ideal chain is strict. ∎

As an immediate corollary, we get the following result which is well known in the context of finite chain rings (see for example [19, Corollary 4.6] or [7, 3.7 Corollary]).

Corollary 2.

Let f∈R⁡[x]f\in R[x] be a residually square-free polynomial. Then R⁡[x]/(f)R[x]/(f) is a principal ideal ring.

We now investigate the structure of the submodules of a finitely generated free RR-module. The next lemma is an adaptation of [25, Lemma 1, p. 246] to the SPIR case.

Lemma 7.

([25, Lemma 1, p. 246]) Let MM be a finitely generated RR-module and NN a submodule of M.M. Then we have NN is finitely generated and νR​(N)≤νR​(M).\nu_{R}(N)\leq\nu_{R}(M).

A matrix D=(di,j)∈Mm×n​(R)D=(d_{i,j})\in M_{m\times n}(R) is called a diagonal matrix if di,j=0d_{i,j}=0 whenever i≠j.i\neq j. Such a matrix can be expressed as D=diag⁡(d1,…,dr),D=\operatorname{diag}(d_{1},\ldots,d_{r}), where r=min⁡{m,n}r=\min\{m,n\} and di=di,id_{i}=d_{i,i} for i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r. According to [3, Theorem 15.24], for every matrix A∈Mm×n​(R)A\in M_{m\times n}(R), there exist invertible matrices PP and QQ and a diagonal matrix D=diag⁡(d1,d2,…,dr)D=\operatorname{diag}(d_{1},d_{2},\ldots,d_{r}) such that A=P​D​Q,A=PDQ, where the diagonal entries satisfy the divisibility relations d1|d2​∣⋯∣​dr.d_{1}\mid d_{2}\mid\cdots\mid d_{r}. The elements d1,d2,…,drd_{1},d_{2},\ldots,d_{r} are uniquely determined up to associates, and DD is called the Smith normal form of AA. A version of the following theorem is given in [10, Proposition 3.2] for the case of finite PIRs.

Theorem 2.

Let FF be a finitely generated free module of rank nn and let ℬ={u1,…,un}\mathcal{B}=\{u_{1},\dots,u_{n}\} be a basis of F.F. For each integer 1≤m≤n,1\leq m\leq n, denote ℳm\mathcal{M}_{m} the set of submodules of FF with a minimal number of generators equals to m.m. Then we have

ℳm={⟨γk1ψ(u1),…,γkmψ(um)⟩|0≤k1,…,km≤ν−1 and ψ∈AutR(F)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{m}=\left\{\langle\gamma^{k_{1}}\psi(u_{1}),\dots,\gamma^{k_{m}}\psi(u_{m})\rangle~|~0\leq k_{1},\dots,k_{m}\leq\nu-1\text{ and }\psi\in\operatorname{Aut}_{R}(F)\right\}.
Proof.

For each automorphism ψ∈AutR⁡(F),\psi\in\operatorname{Aut}_{R}(F), {ψ⁡(u1),…,ψ⁡(um)}\{\psi(u_{1}),\dots,\psi(u_{m})\} is a linearly independent set. Let k1,…,km∈{0,…,ν−1}.k_{1},\dots,k_{m}\in\{0,\dots,\nu-1\}. Denote ℰ\mathcal{E} the set {γk1​ψ​(u1),…,γkm​ψ​(um)}\{\gamma^{k_{1}}\psi(u_{1}),\dots,\gamma^{k_{m}}\psi(u_{m})\} and M=⟨ℰ⟩.M=\langle\mathcal{E}\rangle. Suppose ℰ\mathcal{E} is not a minimal generating set of M.M. W.l.o.g we can then suppose that there exist α2,…,αm∈R\alpha_{2},\dots,\alpha_{m}\in R such that γk1ψ(u1)=∑i=2m\gamma^{k_{1}}\psi(u_{1})=\sum_{i=2}^{m}αi​γki​ψ​(ui),\alpha_{i}\gamma^{k_{i}}\psi(u_{i}), but this implies that γk1=α2​γk2=⋯=αm​γkm=0\gamma^{k_{1}}=\alpha_{2}\gamma^{k_{2}}=\dots=\alpha_{m}\gamma^{k_{m}}=0 which cannot be as k1<ν.k_{1}<\nu. Hence M∈ℳm.M\in\mathcal{M}_{m}.

Conversely, let M∈ℳmM\in\mathcal{M}_{m} with a minimal generating set {v1,…,vm}.\{v_{1},\dots,v_{m}\}. Let A∈Mm×n​(R)A\in M_{m\times n}(R) be the matrix whose rows are the coordinates of v1,…,vm,v_{1},\dots,v_{m}, in the basis ℬ.\mathcal{B}. By [3, Theorem 15.24], let D=diag⁡(d1,d2,…,dm)D=\operatorname{diag}(d_{1},d_{2},\ldots,d_{m}) be the Smith normal from of A,A, and P∈G​Lm​(R)P\in GL_{m}(R) and Q∈G​Ln​(R)Q\in GL_{n}(R) such that A=P​D​Q.A=PDQ. Right-multiplying by QQ corresponds to changing the basis of F,F, while left-multiplying by PP corresponds to changing the minimal generating set of M.M. Hence there exists an automorphism ψ′∈A​u​tR​(F)\psi^{\prime}\in Aut_{R}(F) such that {d1​ψ′​(u1),…,dm​ψ′​(um)}\{d_{1}\psi^{\prime}(u_{1}),\dots,d_{m}\psi^{\prime}(u_{m})\} is a minimal generating set of M.M. But as νR​(M)=m,\nu_{R}(M)=m, that means that no did_{i} is zero, and thus by Lemma 5, for all 1≤i≤m,1\leq i\leq m, there exist 0≤ki≤ν−10\leq k_{i}\leq\nu-1 and a unit di′∈R∖𝔪d^{\prime}_{i}\in R\setminus\mathfrak{m} such that di=γki​di′.d_{i}=\gamma^{k_{i}}d^{\prime}_{i}. Finally, it follows immediately that there exists an automorphism ψ∈A​u​tR​(F)\psi\in Aut_{R}(F) such that {γk1​ψ​(u1),…,γkm​ψ​(um)}\{\gamma^{k_{1}}\psi(u_{1}),\dots,\gamma^{k_{m}}\psi(u_{m})\} is a minimal generating set of M.M. ∎

For a type of submodules of a finitely generated free module, we can say more about their minimal generating sets.

Proposition 8.

Let FF be a finitely generated free RR-module with basis {u1,…,un}.\{u_{1},\dots,u_{n}\}.

  • (a)

    For all 0≤i≤ν−1,0\leq i\leq\nu-1, 𝔪i​F/𝔪i+1​F\mathfrak{m}^{i}F/\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F and F/𝔪​FF/\mathfrak{m}F are isomorphic both as RR-modules and as kk-vector space.

  • (b)

    For all 0≤i≤ν−1,0\leq i\leq\nu-1, the RR-module 𝔪i​F\mathfrak{m}^{i}F has a minimal generating set {γi​u1,…,γi​un}.\{\gamma^{i}u_{1},\dots,\gamma^{i}u_{n}\}. In particular, we have

    νR​(𝔪ν−1​F)=νR​(𝔪ν−2​F)=⋯=νR​(𝔪​F)=rankR​(F).\nu_{R}(\mathfrak{m}^{\nu-1}F)=\nu_{R}(\mathfrak{m}^{\nu-2}F)=\dots=\nu_{R}(\mathfrak{m}F)=\text{rank}_{R}(F). (4)
Proof.

(a) Fix 0≤i≤ν−1,0\leq i\leq\nu-1, and let the map θ:𝔪i​F/𝔪i+1​F⟶F/𝔪​F\theta:\mathfrak{m}^{i}F/\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F\longrightarrow F/\mathfrak{m}F be such that for all w∈F,w\in F, θ⁡(γi​w+𝔪i+1​F)=w+𝔪​F.\theta(\gamma^{i}w+\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F)=w+\mathfrak{m}F. θ\theta is a well-defined RR-linear map. Indeed, the linearity can be checked easily and for all w1,w2∈Fw_{1},w_{2}\in F such that γi​w1−γi​w2∈𝔪i+1​F,\gamma^{i}w_{1}-\gamma^{i}w_{2}\in\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F, we have γi​(w1−w2)∈𝔪i+1​F,\gamma^{i}(w_{1}-w_{2})\in\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F, hence by Lemma 6, w1−w2∈𝔪​F,w_{1}-w_{2}\in\mathfrak{m}F, and thus θ⁡(γi​w1+𝔪i+1​F)=θ⁡(γi​w2+𝔪i+1​F).\theta(\gamma^{i}w_{1}+\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F)=\theta(\gamma^{i}w_{2}+\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F). Moreover, θ\theta is clearly onto, and for all w∈F,w\in F, if w∈𝔪​Fw\in\mathfrak{m}F then γi​w∈𝔪i+1​F,\gamma^{i}w\in\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F, hence θ\theta is one-to-one and thus it is an RR-module isomorphism. On the other hand, endowing 𝔪i​F/𝔪i+1​F\mathfrak{m}^{i}F/\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F with the kk-vector space structure such that for all α∈k,\alpha\in k, if β∈R\beta\in R is such that μ⁡(β)=α\mu(\beta)=\alpha then for each w∈𝔪i​F/𝔪i+1​F,w\in\mathfrak{m}^{i}F/\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F, α​w=β​w,\alpha w=\beta w, we can easily verify that θ\theta is a kk-linear map w.r.t this structure, hence θ\theta is also an isomorphism between kk-vector spaces.

(b) By Theorem 1, {u1+𝔪​F,…,un+𝔪​F}\{u_{1}+\mathfrak{m}F,\dots,u_{n}+\mathfrak{m}F\} is a kk-basis of F/𝔪​F.F/\mathfrak{m}F. Fix 0≤i≤ν−1.0\leq i\leq\nu-1. From the proof of (a) above, we see that {γi​u1+𝔪i+1​F,…,γi​un+𝔪i+1​F}\{\gamma^{i}u_{1}+\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F,\dots,\gamma^{i}u_{n}+\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F\} is a basis of the kk-vector space 𝔪i​F/𝔪i+1​F,\mathfrak{m}^{i}F/\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F, hence by Theorem 1, {γi​u1,…,γi​un}\{\gamma^{i}u_{1},\dots,\gamma^{i}u_{n}\} is a minimal generating set of 𝔪i​F,\mathfrak{m}^{i}F, and νR​(𝔪i​F)=rankR⁡(F).\nu_{R}(\mathfrak{m}^{i}F)=\operatorname{rank}_{R}(F). ∎

Remark 2.

Note that unlike the case of modules of the form 𝔪i​F\mathfrak{m}^{i}F as in Proposition 8, where each basis of FF can be turned into a minimal generating set of 𝔪i​F,\mathfrak{m}^{i}F, for a general submodule M≤FM\leq F with νR​(M)=n,\nu_{R}(M)=n, Theorem 2 only asserts that we can obtain a minimal generating set of MM from a given basis of F.F. Take R=ℤ/8​ℤR=\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z} for example, and let {e1,e2}\{e_{1},e_{2}\} be the canonical basis of R2.R^{2}. Let M=⟨2​(e1+e2),4​e2⟩≤R2M=\langle 2(e_{1}+e_{2}),4e_{2}\rangle\leq R^{2}. We can easily verify that for all 0≤i,j≤2,0\leq i,j\leq 2, M≠⟨2i​e1,2j​e2⟩.M\neq\langle 2^{i}e_{1},2^{j}e_{2}\rangle.

5 Endomorphisms with residually square-free annihilator polynomials

Throughout the remainder of the paper, RR is an SPIR with maximal ideal 𝔪=γ​R,\mathfrak{m}=\gamma R, nilpotency index ν,\nu, and residue field k=R/𝔪,k=R/\mathfrak{m}, FF is a finitely generated free RR-module of rank n∈ℕ,n\in\mathbb{N}, and φ∈EndR​(F).\varphi\in\text{End}_{R}(F).

Let λφ∈Nφ\lambda_{\varphi}\in N_{\varphi} denote a monic polynomial of least degree among the monic polynomials in Nφ.N_{\varphi}. Following Proposition 2, we see that each monic polynomial of least degree in NφN_{\varphi} has the same projection μ⁡(λφ)\mu(\lambda_{\varphi}) in k⁡[x].k[x]. It is easy to see that μ⁡(χφ)=χμ⁡(φ).\mu({\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi})={\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\mu(\varphi)}. On the other hand, denoting λμ⁡(φ)\lambda_{\mu(\varphi)} the minimal polynomial of μ⁡(φ),\mu(\varphi), we have λμ⁡(φ)\lambda_{\mu(\varphi)} divides μ⁡(λφ)\mu(\lambda_{\varphi}) as the latter annihilates μ⁡(φ),\mu(\varphi), however, we do not have in general that μ⁡(λφ)=λμ⁡(φ),\mu(\lambda_{\varphi})=\lambda_{\mu(\varphi)}, and this makes working with φ\varphi quite difficult. To deal with this problem, McDonald introduced the concept of regular endomorphisms over SPIRs in [14] which was generalized later in [8] for an arbitrary commutative local rings. φ\varphi is said to be regular if R⁡[φ]R[\varphi] is a free RR-submodule of EndR​(F).\text{End}_{R}(F). The strength of this notion in the SPIR case, lies in the following proposition.

Proposition 9.

([14, Theorems II.3 and II.4 ]) The Following are equivalent:

  • (i)

    φ\varphi is regular,

  • (ii)

    NφN_{\varphi} is a principal ideal generated by a monic polynomial,

  • (iii)

    μ⁡(λφ)=λμ⁡(φ).\mu(\lambda_{\varphi})=\lambda_{\mu(\varphi)}.

It follows that if φ\varphi is regular, then NφN_{\varphi} has a unique monic polynomial of least degree. We call it the minimal polynomial of φ\varphi and denote it λφ.\lambda_{\varphi}. And so in this case we have Nφ=(λφ).N_{\varphi}=(\lambda_{\varphi}).

Proposition 10.

Suppose there exists a residually square-free polynomial f∈Nφ,f\in N_{\varphi}, and let f=∏1≤i≤rfif=\prod_{1\leq i\leq r}f_{i} be a decomposition of ff into pairwise coprime basic irreducible polynomials. Denote Vi=k​e​r​(fi​(φ))V_{i}=ker(f_{i}(\varphi)) and Vi¯=k​e​r​(μ⁡(fi)​(μ⁡(φ)))\overline{V_{i}}=ker(\mu(f_{i})(\mu(\varphi))) for i∈{1,…,r}.i\in\{1,\dots,r\}. We have the following:

  • (i)

    For each i∈{1,…,r},i\in\{1,\dots,r\}, ViV_{i} is free and invariant under φ,\varphi, and F=⨁i=1rVi.F=\bigoplus^{r}_{i=1}V_{i}. Moreover, if Nφ=(f)N_{\varphi}=(f) then for i=1,…,r,i=1,\dots,r, φ|Vi\varphi_{|V_{i}} is regular with Nφ|Vi=(fi).N_{\varphi_{|V_{i}}}=(f_{i}).

  • (ii)

    For each i∈{1,…,r},i\in\{1,\dots,r\}, Vi¯=μ⁡(Vi)\overline{V_{i}}=\mu(V_{i}) and rankR⁡(Vi)=dim⁡(Vi¯).\operatorname{rank}_{R}(V_{i})=\operatorname{dim}(\overline{V_{i}}). In particular, denoting kik_{i} the multiplicity of μ⁡(fi)\mu(f_{i}) in χμ⁡(φ),{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\mu(\varphi)}, we have rankR⁡(Vi)=ki​deg⁡(fi).\operatorname{rank}_{R}(V_{i})=k_{i}\deg(f_{i}).

Proof.

(i) The proof that F=⨁i=1rViF=\bigoplus^{r}_{i=1}V_{i} with each ViV_{i} invariant under φ\varphi is the same as the case of vector spaces, see [9, Theorem 12, Chapter 6] for example. Moreover, from Proposition 1, each ViV_{i} is free. Now suppose that Nφ=(f).N_{\varphi}=(f). We prove the result for r=2r=2 and the general case follows immediately by induction. From Lemma 2 we can suppose w.l.o.g that ff is monic as well as f1f_{1} and f2.f_{2}. For i=1,2,i=1,2, denote φi=φ↾Vi.\varphi_{i}=\varphi_{\restriction V_{i}}. We have obviously that fi∈Nφi.f_{i}\in N_{\varphi_{i}}. Now suppose there exists g∈Nφ1g\in N_{\varphi_{1}} such that deg⁡(g)<deg⁡(f1).\deg(g)<\deg(f_{1}). As F=V1⊕V2,F=V_{1}\oplus V_{2}, for each v∈Fv\in F there exists v1∈V1v_{1}\in V_{1} and v2∈V2v_{2}\in V_{2} such that v=v1+v2,v=v_{1}+v_{2}, so we have (g​f2)​(φ)​(v)=(g​f2)​(φ1)​(v1)+(g​f2)​(φ2)​(v2)=f2​(φ1)​(g⁡(φ1)​(v1))+g⁡(φ2)​(f2​(φ2)​(v2))=0.(gf_{2})(\varphi)(v)=(gf_{2})(\varphi_{1})(v_{1})+(gf_{2})(\varphi_{2})(v_{2})=f_{2}(\varphi_{1})(g(\varphi_{1})(v_{1}))+g(\varphi_{2})(f_{2}(\varphi_{2})(v_{2}))=0. Hence g​f2∈Nφ=(f),gf_{2}\in N_{\varphi}=(f), but as deg⁡(g)<deg⁡(f1),\deg(g)<\deg(f_{1}), deg⁡(g​f2)<deg⁡(f)\deg(gf_{2})<\deg(f) which implies that g​f2=0,gf_{2}=0, and as f2f_{2} is monic this means that g=0.g=0. f1f_{1} is then of minimal degree among the nonzero polynomials of Nφ1,N_{\varphi_{1}}, hence by Euclidean division, as f1f_{1} is monic, Nφ1=(f1).N_{\varphi_{1}}=(f_{1}). The case of φ2\varphi_{2} follows by symmetry.

(ii) Same proof as the one given for finite chain rings in [16, 3.5. Proposition]. ∎

A standard theorem in linear algebra states that the minimal polynomial of a block diagonal matrix is the least common multiple of the minimal polynomials of its diagonal blocks. We adapt this result to our context as follows.

Proposition 11.

Suppose there exists a residually square-free polynomial ff in NφN_{\varphi}. If FF is a direct sum of φ\varphi-invariant submodules such that the restriction of φ\varphi to each summand is a regular endomorphism, then φ\varphi is regular.

Proof.

As μ⁡(f)\mu(f) is square-free, by Lemma 2 we can take ff to be monic w.l.o.g. Let f=∏i=1rfif=\prod_{i=1}^{r}f_{i} be the unique factorization of ff into monic pairwise coprime basic irreducible polynomials. As RR is local, each summand of the direct sum is free, hence there exists a basis ℬ\mathcal{B} of FF relative to which the matrix of φ\varphi is of the form d​i​a​g​(M1,…,Mq)diag(M_{1},\dots,M_{q}) for some regular matrices M1,…,Mq.M_{1},\dots,M_{q}. It is easy to see that μ⁡(φ)\mu(\varphi) is represented by d​i​a​g​(μ⁡(M1),…,μ⁡(Mq))diag(\mu(M_{1}),\dots,\mu(M_{q})) in the ordered basis μ⁡(ℬ)\mu(\mathcal{B}) of F/𝔪​F,F/\mathfrak{m}F, hence the minimal polynomial of μ⁡(φ)\mu(\varphi) is l.c.m​(λμ⁡(M1),…,λμ⁡(Mq)).\text{l.c.m}(\lambda_{\mu(M_{1})},\dots,\lambda_{\mu(M_{q})}). For each i∈{1,…,q},i\in\{1,\dots,q\}, as MiM_{i} is regular and annihilated by f,f, we have μ⁡(λMi)=λμ⁡(Mi)\mu(\lambda_{M_{i}})=\lambda_{\mu(M_{i})} and λMi\lambda_{M_{i}} divides f,f, so by the uniqueness of the irreducible decomposition of Proposition 4, there exists a subset Ji⊂{1,…,r}J_{i}\subset\{1,\dots,r\} such that λMi=∏j∈Jifj.\lambda_{M_{i}}=\prod_{j\in J_{i}}f_{j}. Let J=∪1≤i≤qJiJ=\cup_{1\leq i\leq q}J_{i} and denote g=∏i∈Jfi.g=\prod_{i\in J}f_{i}. We have g∈Nφg\in N_{\varphi} and μ⁡(g)=l.c.m​(μ⁡(λM1),…,μ⁡(λMq))=l.c.m​(λμ⁡(M1),…,λμ⁡(Mq))=λμ⁡(φ),\mu(g)=\text{l.c.m}(\mu(\lambda_{M_{1}}),\dots,\mu(\lambda_{M_{q}}))=\text{l.c.m}(\lambda_{\mu(M_{1})},\dots,\lambda_{\mu(M_{q})})=\lambda_{\mu(\varphi)}, hence by Proposition 9, φ\varphi is regular. ∎

Next, we consider the case where the characteristic polynomial is residually square-free.

Proposition 12.

If μ⁡(χφ)\mu({\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi}) is square-free, then φ\varphi is regular and Nφ=(χφ).N_{\varphi}=({\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi}). Furthermore, there exists an element w∈Fw\in F such that ℬ={w,φ⁡(w),…,φn−1​(w)}\mathcal{B}=\{w,\varphi(w),\dots,\varphi^{n-1}(w)\} is a basis of FF and φ\varphi is represented in ℬ\mathcal{B} by c​o​m​(χφ)com({\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi}).

Proof.

As μ⁡(χφ)=χμ⁡(φ),\mu({\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi})={\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\mu(\varphi)}, if μ⁡(χφ)\mu({\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi}) is square-free, then χμ⁡(φ)=λμ⁡(φ),{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\mu(\varphi)}=\lambda_{\mu(\varphi)}, which implies by Proposition 9(iii) that φ\varphi is regular and Nφ=(χφ)N_{\varphi}=({\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi}). Moreover, as χμ⁡(φ)=λμ⁡(φ),{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\mu(\varphi)}=\lambda_{\mu(\varphi)}, there exists an element w∈Fw\in F such that {w+𝔪​F,μ⁡(φ)​(w+𝔪​F),…,μ​(φ)n−1​(w+𝔪​F)}\{w+\mathfrak{m}F,\mu(\varphi)(w+\mathfrak{m}F),\dots,\mu(\varphi)^{n-1}(w+\mathfrak{m}F)\} is a basis of F/𝔪​FF/\mathfrak{m}F (see [9, page 237, Corollary]). Hence, as μ​(φ)i​(w+𝔪​F)=φi​(w)+𝔪​F\mu(\varphi)^{i}(w+\mathfrak{m}F)=\varphi^{i}(w)+\mathfrak{m}F for all i,i, by Corollary 1 we have that {w,φ⁡(w),…,φn−1​(w)}\{w,\varphi(w),\dots,\varphi^{n-1}(w)\} is linearly independent in F,F, which implies by Proposition 5(ii) that it is a basis of F,F, and it is easy to check that φ\varphi is represented by c​o​m​(χφ)com({\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi}) in it. ∎

In [14, Theorem III.2], it was claimed that each regular endomorphism of FF can be represented by a matrix that splits as a sum of companion matrices diag​(C1,…,Cr)\text{diag}(C_{1},\dots,C_{r}) for some companion matrices C1,…,Cr.C_{1},\dots,C_{r}. This was soon after shown to be false, (see e.g. [8, 17]). However, the next proposition shows that it holds when the minimal polynomial of the endomorphism is residually square-free.

Proposition 13.

If φ\varphi has a residually square-free annihilating polynomial, then a basis of FF may be chosen wherein φ\varphi is represented by a matrix that splits as a sum of companion matrices.

Proof.

From [17, Theorem 1], we have that φ\varphi may be represented by a matrix that splits as a sum of companion matrices if and only if the R⁡[x]R[x]-module M⁡(φ)M(\varphi) decomposes into a direct sum of cyclic modules, hence all we need to prove is that M⁡(φ)M(\varphi) has such decomposition. Let f∈Nφf\in N_{\varphi} be such that μ⁡(f)\mu(f) is square-free. As (f)⊆AnnR⁡[x]⁡(M⁡(φ)),(f)\subseteq\operatorname{Ann}_{R[x]}(M(\varphi)), M⁡(φ)M(\varphi) can be considered as a module over R⁡[x]/(f)R[x]/(f) in a natural way, moreover, it decomposes as a direct sum of cyclic modules as an R⁡[x]R[x]-module if and only if it does as an R⁡[x]/(f)R[x]/(f)-module. But as μ⁡(f)\mu(f) is square-free, R⁡[x]/(f)R[x]/(f) is a PIR by Corollary 2. Hence by the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PIR [3, Theorem 15.33], as an R⁡[x]/(f)R[x]/(f)-module, M⁡(φ)M(\varphi) is a direct sum of cyclic modules. ∎

Combining the previous propositions yields the following important result.

Theorem 3.

If there exists f∈Nφf\in N_{\varphi} such that μ⁡(f)\mu(f) is square-free then φ\varphi is regular, and Nφ=(g)N_{\varphi}=(g) for some monic polynomial g∈R⁡[x]g\in R[x] that divides f.f.

Proof.

Following Proposition 13, let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a basis of FF relative to which the matrix of φ\varphi is diag​(C1,…,Cr)\text{diag}(C_{1},\dots,C_{r}) for some companion matrices C1,…,Cr.C_{1},\dots,C_{r}. Fix an integer 1≤i≤r.1\leq i\leq r. It is easy to see that f∈NCi,f\in N_{C_{i}}, hence μ⁡(f)\mu(f) annihilates μ⁡(Ci).\mu(C_{i}). But as CiC_{i} is a companion matrix, so is μ⁡(Ci),\mu(C_{i}), hence χμ⁡(Ci)=λμ⁡(Ci){\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\mu(C_{i})}=\lambda_{\mu(C_{i})} which implies that χμ⁡(Ci){\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\mu(C_{i})} divides μ⁡(f).\mu(f). We have then χμ⁡(Ci){\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\mu(C_{i})} is square-free, but as χμ⁡(Ci)=μ⁡(χCi),{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\mu(C_{i})}=\mu({\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{C_{i}}), using Proposition 12 we see that CiC_{i} is regular. Finally, by Proposition 11, φ\varphi is also regular. ∎

Corollary 3.

φ\varphi has a residually square-free annihilating polynomial if and only if μ⁡(λφ)\mu(\lambda_{\varphi}) is square-free.

Proof.

Suppose there exists f∈Nφf\in N_{\varphi} such that μ⁡(f)\mu(f) is square-free. We have then by Theorem 3, φ\varphi is regular. Hence Nφ=(λφ)N_{\varphi}=(\lambda_{\varphi}) and λφ\lambda_{\varphi} divides f.f. We have then μ⁡(λφ)\mu(\lambda_{\varphi}) divides μ⁡(f)\mu(f) and thus it is square-free. The converse is immediate, since λφ∈Nφ.\lambda_{\varphi}\in N_{\varphi}. ∎

Remark 3.

The condition that not only the annihilating polynomial is square-free but also its projection modulo 𝔪,\mathfrak{m}, is necessary for the theorem to hold. Over the SPIR R=ℤ/8​ℤR=\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z} for example, the matrix A=(2004)A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\ 0&4\end{pmatrix} is annihilated by the polynomial (x−2)​(x−4)(x-2)(x-4) which is easily verified to be square-free, however it is not regular. Indeed, as μ⁡(A)=0,\mu(A)=0, λμ⁡(A)=x,\lambda_{\mu(A)}=x, so for AA to be regular we must have that AA is annihilated by a polynomial of the form x−αx-\alpha with α\alpha a zero-divisor in R,R, and it is easy to see that it is not the case.

Remark 4.

(Converse of Proposition 11) Let WW be a free φ\varphi-invariant submodule of F.F. An annihilating polynomial of φ\varphi obviously annihilates φ↾W.\varphi_{\restriction W}. Hence if φ\varphi has a residually square-free annihilating polynomial, then so does φ↾W,\varphi_{\restriction W}, and by Theorem 3, φ↾W\varphi_{\restriction W} is also regular.

Notation 1.

For the rest of this paper, we assume that φ\varphi has a residually square-free annihilating polynomial. In light of Theorem 3 and Corollary 3, this means that λφ\lambda_{\varphi} is unique and residually square-free, so by Proposition 4 let λφ=∏i=1rfi\lambda_{\varphi}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}f_{i} be the factorization of λφ\lambda_{\varphi} into monic basic irreducible pairwise coprime polynomials, and let m1,…,mr∈ℕ∗m_{1},\dots,m_{r}\in\mathbb{N}^{*} be such that χμ⁡(φ)=∏i=1rμ​(fi)mi.{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\mu(\varphi)}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\mu(f_{i})^{m_{i}}. Moreover, for all 1≤i≤r,1\leq i\leq r, denote Vi=k​e​r​(fi​(φ)),V_{i}=ker(f_{i}(\varphi)), and φi\varphi_{i} the restriction of φ\varphi to Vi.V_{i}.

Recall that a linear operator T:V→VT:V\rightarrow V on a vector space VV is called semisimple, if every TT-invariant subspace has a TT-invariant complement. In light of this and Proposition 1, we give the following definition of a semisimple endomorphism of F.F.

Definition 1.

An endomorphism ψ∈EndR​(F)\psi\in\text{End}_{R}(F) is said to be semisimple if every free ψ\psi-invariant submodule of FF has a ψ\psi-invariant complement.

We conclude this section by showing that φ\varphi is a semisimple endomorphism. We start with the following two propositions which will be useful throughout the remainder of the paper.

Proposition 14.

For each φ\varphi-invariant submodule WW of F,F, we have

  • (i)

    W=⨁i=1rW∩Vi,W=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}W\cap V_{i},

  • (ii)

    for all 1≤i≤r,1\leq i\leq r, W∩ViW\cap V_{i} is invariant under φ,\varphi,

  • (iii)

    WW is free if and only if W∩ViW\cap V_{i} is free for all i.i.

Proof.

(i) Let w∈W.w\in W. From Proposition 10, we have that F=⨁1≤i≤rVi,F=\bigoplus_{1\leq i\leq r}V_{i}, hence, for all i,i, there exists a unique wi∈Viw_{i}\in V_{i} such that w=w1+⋯+wr.w=w_{1}+\dots+w_{r}. For all 1≤i≤r,1\leq i\leq r, let fi^=∏1≤j≤rj≠ifj.\hat{f_{i}}=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j\leq r\\ j\neq i\end{subarray}}f_{j}. As the fif_{i}’s are pairwise coprime, fif_{i} and fi^\hat{f_{i}} are also coprime, so for all i,i, there exist αi,βi∈R⁡[x]\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\in R[x] such that αi​fi+βi​fi^=1.\alpha_{i}f_{i}+\beta_{i}\hat{f_{i}}=1. Take the case of i=1i=1 for example. We have f1^​(φ)​(w)=∑j=1rf1^​(φ)​(wj)=f1^​(φ)​(w1),\hat{f_{1}}(\varphi)(w)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\hat{f_{1}}(\varphi)(w_{j})=\hat{f_{1}}(\varphi)(w_{1}), moreover, (α1​f1)​(φ)​(w1)+(β1​f1^)​(φ)​(w1)=w1,(\alpha_{1}f_{1})(\varphi)(w_{1})+(\beta_{1}\hat{f_{1}})(\varphi)(w_{1})=w_{1}, hence as w1∈V1,w_{1}\in V_{1}, (β1​f1^)​(φ)​(w1)=w1,(\beta_{1}\hat{f_{1}})(\varphi)(w_{1})=w_{1}, and thus (β1​f1^)​(φ)​(w)=w1,(\beta_{1}\hat{f_{1}})(\varphi)(w)=w_{1}, which means that w1∈W∩V1,w_{1}\in W\cap V_{1}, as WW is invariant under φ\varphi and w∈W.w\in W. So by symmetry, for all 1≤i≤r,1\leq i\leq r, wi∈W∩Vi,w_{i}\in W\cap V_{i}, and thus W=W∩V1+⋯+W∩Vr.W=W\cap V_{1}+\dots+W\cap V_{r}. Moreover, as the ViV_{i}’s are in a direct sum we get W=W∩V1⊕⋯⊕W∩Vr.W=W\cap V_{1}\oplus\dots\oplus W\cap V_{r}.

(ii) As both WW and the ViV_{i}’s are φ\varphi-invariant, it is clear that the W∩ViW\cap V_{i}’s are φ\varphi-invariant too.

(iii) If W∩ViW\cap V_{i} is free for all ii then WW is obviously free too. The converse follows from Proposition 1. ∎

Proposition 15.

Suppose that μ⁡(λφ)\mu(\lambda_{\varphi}) is irreducible. Then M⁡(φ),M(\varphi), the module associated with φ,\varphi, is free as an R⁡[x]/(λφ)R[x]/(\lambda_{\varphi})-module.

Proof.

As μ⁡(λφ)\mu(\lambda_{\varphi}) is irreducible, by Theorem 3, φ\varphi is regular and Nφ=(λφ).N_{\varphi}=(\lambda_{\varphi}). It is clear that (λφ)(\lambda_{\varphi}) is the annihilator of M⁡(φ),M(\varphi), and thus M⁡(φ)M(\varphi) can naturally be viewed as an R⁡[x]/(λφ)R[x]/(\lambda_{\varphi}) module. Denote SS the ring R⁡[x]/(λφ).R[x]/(\lambda_{\varphi}). By Proposition 7, SS is an SPIR with ideals γk​S=(γk+(λφ))\gamma^{k}S=(\gamma^{k}+(\lambda_{\varphi})) for 0≤k≤ν.0\leq k\leq\nu. We have then by the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PIR [3, Theorem 15.33], there exist an integer qq and k1≤⋯≤kqk_{1}\leq\dots\leq k_{q} in {1,…,ν}\{1,\dots,\nu\} such that M⁡(φ)≃⨁1≤i≤qS/γki​S.M(\varphi)\simeq\bigoplus_{1\leq i\leq q}S/\gamma^{k_{i}}S. Hence, as RR-modules, F≃⨁1≤i≤qS/γki​S,F\simeq\bigoplus_{1\leq i\leq q}S/\gamma^{k_{i}}S, and thus, by Proposition 1, for all 1≤i≤q,1\leq i\leq q, S/γki​SS/\gamma^{k_{i}}S is a free RR-module, which implies that there exists an element wi∈S/γki​Sw_{i}\in S/\gamma^{k_{i}}S such that γν−1​wi≠0,\gamma^{\nu-1}w_{i}\neq 0, but as AnnS​(S/γki​S)=γki​S,\text{Ann}_{S}(S/\gamma^{k_{i}}S)=\gamma^{k_{i}}S, this means that for all i,i, ki=ν,k_{i}=\nu, and thus M⁡(φ)≃SqM(\varphi)\simeq S^{q} is a free SS-module. ∎

Theorem 4.

The endomorphism φ\varphi is semisimple.

Proof.

Let WW be a free φ\varphi-invariant submodule of F.F. From Proposition 14 we have that W=⨁i=1rW∩ViW=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}W\cap V_{i} with each W∩ViW\cap V_{i} free and φ\varphi-invariant. Hence to prove that WW have a φ\varphi-invariant complement, it suffices to prove that for each i,i, W∩ViW\cap V_{i} has a φ\varphi-invariant complement in Vi.V_{i}. We can then w.l.o.g suppose that λφ\lambda_{\varphi} is basic irreducible. Denote SS the ring R⁡[x]/(λφ).R[x]/(\lambda_{\varphi}). Since WW is free and φ↾W\varphi_{\restriction W} is regular of minimal polynomial λφ,\lambda_{\varphi}, by Proposition 15, WW can be seen as a free SS-submodule of M⁡(φ).M(\varphi). Moreover, from Proposition 7, SS is an SPIR, hence it is weakly semi-Steinitz and by Proposition 5(iii), there exists an SS-submodule W′W^{\prime} of M⁡(φ)M(\varphi) such that M⁡(φ)=W⊕W′.M(\varphi)=W\oplus W^{\prime}. But since W′W^{\prime} is an R⁡[x]/(λφ)R[x]/(\lambda_{\varphi})-submodule of M⁡(φ),M(\varphi), it can be seen as a φ\varphi-invariant RR-module, hence as RR-modules, F=W⊕W′F=W\oplus W^{\prime} with W′W^{\prime} φ\varphi-invariant. ∎

Remark 5.

While an endomorphism of a finite dimensional vector space is semisimple if and only if its minimal polynomial is square-free (see [9, Theorem 11, Chapter 7]), the converse of Theorem 4 does not hold, as shown by the following counterexample. Let R=ℤ/4​ℤR=\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z} and consider the matrix A=(0120)∈M2​(R).A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 2&0\end{pmatrix}\in M_{2}(R). It is easy to see that λA=x2−2,\lambda_{A}=x^{2}-2, and μ⁡(λA)=x2\mu(\lambda_{A})=x^{2} is not square-free. We claim that R2R^{2} has no nonzero proper free φA\varphi_{A}-invariant submodules. Indeed otherwise, let MM be such a submodule. As the rank of MM must be 1,1, let w=(w1,w2)∈R2w=(w_{1},w_{2})\in R^{2} such that M=R​wM=Rw and μ⁡(w)≠0.\mu(w)\neq 0. We have then φA​(w)=(w2,2​w1)∈M\varphi_{A}(w)=(w_{2},2w_{1})\in M which means that there exists α∈R\alpha\in R such that w2=α​w1w_{2}=\alpha w_{1} and 2​w1=α​w22w_{1}=\alpha w_{2} and this implies that w1,w2∈2​Rw_{1},w_{2}\in 2R which contradicts the assumption that μ⁡(w)≠0.\mu(w)\neq 0. We have then, φA\varphi_{A} is trivially semisimple despite the fact that μ⁡(λA)\mu(\lambda_{A}) is not square-free.

6 Invariant submodules

We begin our investigation of the φ\varphi-invariant submodules of FF by considering the simplest type, namely, the smallest φ\varphi-invariant submodule containing a given element of F.F.

Definition 2.

For each w∈F,w\in F, the φ\varphi-cyclic submodule of FF generated by ww is the submodule of all elements of the form g​(φ)​(w)g(\varphi)(w) with g∈R⁡[x].g\in R[x]. We denote it Z⁡(w,φ).Z(w,\varphi).

For an element w∈F,w\in F, Z⁡(w,φ)Z(w,\varphi) can be viewed as an R⁡[x]R[x]-submodule of M⁡(φ),M(\varphi), the R⁡[x]R[x]-module associated with φ.\varphi. In this setting it is easy to see that Z⁡(w,φ)Z(w,\varphi) corresponds to the cyclic module generated by ww in M⁡(φ),M(\varphi), and conversely, for each w∈M⁡(φ),w\in M(\varphi), R⁡[x]​wR[x]w corresponds to Z⁡(w,φ).Z(w,\varphi).

For a kk-vector space VV and ψ∈Endk​(V),\psi\in\text{End}_{k}(V), for each vector w∈V,w\in V, we denote Nψ​(w)N_{\psi}(w) the ideal of k⁡[x]k[x] such that p∈Nψ​(w)p\in N_{\psi}(w) if and only p​(ψ)​(w)=0.p(\psi)(w)=0. The next lemma uses the fact that for each w∈F,w\in F, Nμ⁡(φ)​(w+𝔪​F)N_{\mu(\varphi)}(w+\mathfrak{m}F) is a principal ideal that contains 11 if and only if w∈𝔪​F.w\in\mathfrak{m}F.

Lemma 8.

Suppose that λφ\lambda_{\varphi} is basic irreducible. Then for each nonzero element w∈F,w\in F, the set ℬ={φi​(w)|0≤i≤deg⁡(λφ)−1}\mathcal{B}=\{\varphi^{i}(w)~|~0\leq i\leq\deg(\lambda_{\varphi})-1\} is a minimal generating set of Z⁡(w,φ).Z(w,\varphi). Suppose at first that w∉𝔪​F.w\notin\mathfrak{m}F. As λφ​(φ)​(w)=0\lambda_{\varphi}(\varphi)(w)=0 and λφ\lambda_{\varphi} is monic, it is clear that ℬ\mathcal{B} generates Z⁡(w,φ).Z(w,\varphi). But from Diagram 1, we see that μ⁡(ℬ)={μ⁡(φi)​(w+𝔪​F)|0≤i≤deg⁡(λφ)−1}={μ​(φ)i​(w+𝔪​F)|0≤i≤deg⁡(λφ)−1}.\mu(\mathcal{B})=\{\mu(\varphi^{i})(w+\mathfrak{m}F)~|~0\leq i\leq\deg(\lambda_{\varphi})-1\}=\{\mu(\varphi)^{i}(w+\mathfrak{m}F)~|~0\leq i\leq\deg(\lambda_{\varphi})-1\}. Hence, μ⁡(ℬ)\mu(\mathcal{B}) being dependent means that there exists a monic polynomial f∈k⁡[x]f\in k[x] such that deg⁡(f)≤deg⁡(λφ)−1\deg(f)\leq\deg(\lambda_{\varphi})-1 and f⁡(μ⁡(φ))​(w+𝔪​F)=0,f(\mu(\varphi))(w+\mathfrak{m}F)=0, i.e. f∈Nμ⁡(φ)​(w+𝔪​F).f\in N_{\mu(\varphi)}(w+\mathfrak{m}F). As w∉𝔪​F,w\notin\mathfrak{m}F, Nμ⁡(φ)​(w+𝔪​F)≠k⁡[x],N_{\mu(\varphi)}(w+\mathfrak{m}F)\neq k[x], hence as the irreducible polynomial μ⁡(λφ)\mu(\lambda_{\varphi}) is in Nμ⁡(φ)​(w+𝔪​F)N_{\mu(\varphi)}(w+\mathfrak{m}F) we have Nμ⁡(φ)​(w+𝔪​F)=(μ⁡(λφ)),N_{\mu(\varphi)}(w+\mathfrak{m}F)=(\mu(\lambda_{\varphi})), and that implies that f∈(μ⁡(λφ))f\in(\mu(\lambda_{\varphi})) which contradicts the fact that deg⁡(f)≤deg⁡(λφ)−1.\deg(f)\leq\deg(\lambda_{\varphi})-1. We have then Z⁡(w,φ)Z(w,\varphi) is a free submodule of FF with basis ℬ.\mathcal{B}. Moreover, φ↾Z⁡(w,φ)\varphi_{\restriction Z(w,\varphi)} is annihilated by λφ,\lambda_{\varphi}, hence by Theorem 3, it is regular, and as rankR⁡(Z⁡(w,φ))=deg⁡(λφ)\operatorname{rank}_{R}(Z(w,\varphi))=\deg(\lambda_{\varphi}) and λφ\lambda_{\varphi} is irreducible, λφ↾Z⁡(w,φ)=χφ↾Z⁡(w,φ)=λφ.\lambda_{\varphi_{\restriction Z(w,\varphi)}}={\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi_{\restriction Z(w,\varphi)}}=\lambda_{\varphi}.

Remark 7.

An endomorphism with no residually square-free annihilating polynomial may have a characteristic polynomial that cannot be expressed as a product of basic irreducible polynomials. Indeed, by use of the companion matrix, each monic polynomial of degree equal to the rank of FF is the characteristic polynomial for some endomorphism of F.F. And in the ring R=ℤ/4​ℤR=\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z} for example, x2+2x^{2}+2 cannot be written as a product of basic irreducible polynomials.

We end this section by considering the question of similarity in the context of matrices with residually square-free annihilating polynomials. The next theorem generalizes the results of [6] from ℤ/pn​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p^{n}\mathbb{Z} to SPIRs.

Theorem 7.

Let A,B∈Mn​(R)A,B\in M_{n}(R) be two matrices with residually square-free annihilating polynomials. The following are equivalent:

    AA and BB are similar,

  • (iii)

    λA=λB\lambda_{A}=\lambda_{B} and χA=χB,{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{A}={\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{B},

  • (iv)

Hence from Corollary 7, as λA=λB,\lambda_{A}=\lambda_{B}, we have that χA=χB.{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{A}={\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{B}.

Remark 8.

While over a field, two linear operators with square-free minimal polynomials are similar if and only if their characteristic polynomials are equal, this does not hold for RR in general. This stems from the fact that R⁡[x]R[x] is not always a UFD and the characteristic polynomial can have multiple factorizations into basic irreducible polynomials. Consider for example R=ℤ/4​ℤ,R=\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}, and let A=(3003).A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\ 0&3\end{pmatrix}. We have that both AA and I2I_{2} have residually square-free annihilating polynomials and χA=(x−3)2=(x−1)2=χI2,{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{A}=(x-3)^{2}=(x-1)^{2}={\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{I_{2}}, yet λA=x−3≠λI2=x−1,\lambda_{A}=x-3\neq\lambda_{I_{2}}=x-1, which means that AA and I2I_{2} cannot be similar.

7 Invariance in the non-derogatory case

A regular endomorphism such that the minimal and characteristic polynomials coincide is said to be non-derogatory. We devote this section to investigating this special case.

Lemma 10.

Suppose that φ\varphi is non-derogatory and that λφ\lambda_{\varphi} is basic irreducible. We have

{Z⁡(w,φ)|w∈F}={𝔪i​F|0≤i≤ν}.\{Z(w,\varphi)~|~w\in F\}=\{\mathfrak{m}^{i}F~|~0\leq i\leq\nu\}. (9)

In particular, for w∈F,w\in F, if ii is an integer such that w∈𝔪i​F∖𝔪i+1​Fw\in\mathfrak{m}^{i}F\setminus\mathfrak{m}^{i+1}F then Z⁡(w,φ)=𝔪i​F.Z(w,\varphi)=\mathfrak{m}^{i}F.

Proof.

Let w∈F.w\in F. Following Lemma 5, let 0≤i≤ν0\leq i\leq\nu and w′∈Fw^{\prime}\in F such that w=γi​w′w=\gamma^{i}w^{\prime} and μ⁡(w′)≠0.\mu(w^{\prime})\neq 0. By Lemma 8, we have that Z⁡(w′,φ)Z(w^{\prime},\varphi) is free and of rank deg⁡(λφ).\deg(\lambda_{\varphi}). But as φ\varphi is non-derogatory deg⁡(λφ)=deg⁡(χφ)=r​a​n​kR​(F).\deg(\lambda_{\varphi})=\deg({\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\chi$}}}_{\varphi})=rank_{R}(F). Hence F=Z⁡(w′,φ)F=Z(w^{\prime},\varphi) which implies that 𝔪i​F=𝔪i​Z​(w′,φ)=Z⁡(γi​w′,φ)=Z⁡(w,φ).\mathfrak{m}^{i}F=\mathfrak{m}^{i}Z(w^{\prime},\varphi)=Z(\gamma^{i}w^{\prime},\varphi)=Z(w,\varphi). Conversely, it is easy to see by Lemma 8, that for all 0≤i≤ν,0\leq i\leq\nu, for each w∈F∖𝔪​F,w\in F\setminus\mathfrak{m}F, Z⁡(γi​w,φ)=𝔪i​F.Z(\gamma^{i}w,\varphi)=\mathfrak{m}^{i}F. ∎

Theorem 8.

Suppose that φ\varphi is non-derogatory, and denote ℐ⁡(φ)\mathcal{I}(\varphi) the set of φ\varphi-invariant submodules of F.F. We have then ℐ⁡(φ)={Z⁡(w,φ)|w∈F}.\mathcal{I}(\varphi)=\left\{Z(w,\varphi)~|~w\in F\right\}. Moreover, every φ\varphi-invariant submodule WW of FF is of the form

W=⨁i=1r𝔪ki​k​e​r​(fi​(φ))with ​0≤ki≤ν, for all ​i.W=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}\mathfrak{m}^{k_{i}}ker(f_{i}(\varphi))~~~~~~~~\text{with }0\leq k_{i}\leq\nu,\text{ for all }i. (10)
Proof.

Obviously, each φ\varphi-cyclic submodule of FF is φ\varphi-invariant. Conversely, let W≤FW\leq F be a φ\varphi-invariant submodule. As φ\varphi is non-derogatory, from Theorem 5, for all 1≤i≤r,1\leq i\leq r, there exists an element wi∈Viw_{i}\in V_{i} such that W=⨁i=1rZ⁡(wi,φ),W=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}Z(w_{i},\varphi), which implies by Lemma 9 that W=Z⁡(w1+⋯+wr,φ).W=Z(w_{1}+\dots+w_{r},\varphi).

Equation (10) follows then immediately from lemmas 9 and 10. ∎

Remark 9.

A polycyclic code of length nn associated to a polynomial ff over a finite chain ring RR can be seen as a submodule of RnR^{n} that is invariant under the action of the matrix com⁡(f).\operatorname{com}(f). When ff is residually square-free, the previous theorem corrects a result given in [2, Theorem 4.2] concerning the structure of the polycyclic codes associated to f,f, where each kik_{i} in Equation (10) was taken to be either ν\nu or 0.0.

The next corollary follows immediately.

Corollary 8.

Suppose that φ\varphi is non-derogatory. The following hold.

  • (a)

    {Vi|1≤i≤r}\{V_{i}~|~1\leq i\leq r\} is the set of all minimal nonzero free φ\varphi-invariant submodule of F.F.

  • (b)

    Every free φ\varphi-invariant submodule of FF is of the form ⨁j∈JVj\bigoplus_{j\in J}V_{j} with J⊆{1,…,r}.J\subseteq\{1,\dots,r\}.

  • (c)

    There are (ν+1)r(\nu+1)^{r} φ\varphi-invariant submodules of F,F, among which 2r2^{r} are free.

Recall that a submodule WW of FF is called φ\varphi-hyperinvariant if it is invariant under every RR-module endomorphism ψ∈EndR​(F)\psi\in\text{End}_{R}(F) that commutes with φ.\varphi.

Proposition 19.

Suppose that φ\varphi is non-derogatory. Then every φ\varphi-invariant submodule WW of FF is φ\varphi-hyperinvariant.

Proof.

Let WW be a φ\varphi-invariant submodule of FF and let ψ\psi be an endomorphism of FF that commutes with φ.\varphi. Following Theorem 8, let k1,…,kr∈ℕk_{1},\dots,k_{r}\in\mathbb{N} such that W=⨁i=1r𝔪ki​Vi.W=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}\mathfrak{m}^{k_{i}}V_{i}. We have then that for every element w∈W,w\in W, for each 1≤i≤r,1\leq i\leq r, there exists wi∈Viw_{i}\in V_{i} such that w=⨁i=1rγki​wi.w=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}\gamma^{k_{i}}w_{i}. On the other hand, ψ\psi commutes with every polynomial in φ,\varphi, hence we have for all i,i, fi​(φ)​(ψ⁡(wi))=ψ⁡(fi​(φ)​(wi))=0,f_{i}(\varphi)(\psi(w_{i}))=\psi(f_{i}(\varphi)(w_{i}))=0, which implies that ψ⁡(wi)∈Vi.\psi(w_{i})\in V_{i}. We have then, ψ⁡(w)=ψ⁡(∑i=1rγki​wi)=∑i=1rγki​ψ​(wi)∈⨁i=1r𝔪ki​Vi=W,\psi(w)=\psi\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}\gamma^{k_{i}}w_{i}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\gamma^{k_{i}}\psi(w_{i})\in\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}\mathfrak{m}^{k_{i}}V_{i}=W, and thus WW is ψ\psi-invariant. ∎
